STMicroelectronics N.V. (NYSE:STM) reported a mixed third quarter on Thursday.

The semiconductor supplier to Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) reported revenue of $3.76 billion, up 17.9% from a year earlier and ahead of the analyst consensus estimate of $3.72 billion, according to Benzinga Pro. Sales to original equipment manufacturers increased 10.2%, while distribution sales rose 38.8%.

Margins Improve As Profitability Recovers

Adjusted earnings were 37 cents per share, missing analysts’ estimate of 39 cents.

Gross margin expanded 410 basis points year over year to 37.3%, above the midpoint of the company’s guidance, helped by lower unused-capacity charges and a more favorable product mix. Operating margin improved 420 basis points to 9.8%.

Net income totaled $291 million, while operating income was $367 million.

Operating income included $55 million of impairment, restructuring and phase-out costs tied primarily to the company’s manufacturing footprint and cost-reduction program, along with $7 million of purchase price accounting effects related to the acquisition of NXP’s MEMS sensor business. Excluding those items, adjusted operating income was $429 million.

STMicroelectronics Segment Performance Shows Broad-Based Growth

Revenue in the Analog, MEMS and Sensors segment rose 8.8% to $1.56 billion, while Embedded Processing revenue increased 24.1% to $1.21 billion.

Power and Discrete revenue grew 11.3% to $477 million, and RF & Optical Communications revenue climbed 46.2% to $504 million.

Boosts Cash Flow

Operating cash flow increased to $1.02 billion from $549 million a year earlier. The company generated $351 million in free cash flow, compared with $130 million in the prior-year period.

STMicroelectronics ended the quarter with a net financial position of $2.11 billion, total liquidity of $5.31 billion and total financial debt of $3.21 billion.

Organizational Restructuring

STMicroelectronics said it will implement a new organizational structure from Jan. 1, 2027, aimed at improving coordination across strategy, technology and product development.

The company named Remi El-Ouazzane as CTO with broader R&D oversight, while Marco Cassis will become Chief Strategic Officer and retain responsibility for identifying growth, partnership and bolt-on M&A opportunities. The rest of the organization will remain unchanged, with implementation due by the end of March 2027.

STMicroelectronics executives said strengthening AI infrastructure demand, an industrial recovery and improving automotive trends are driving growth, while capacity constraints and higher input costs remain key challenges.

CEO Jean-Marc Chéry said demand strengthened during the third quarter, with bookings rising sequentially and the companywide book-to-bill ratio remaining well above 2. Demand exceeded available supply across several product categories, while distributor inventories remained below ST’s normal target.

AI Data Centers And Satellites Drive Growth

Chéry identified AI data centers and low-Earth-orbit satellite communications as major company-specific growth drivers. STMicroelectronics expects AI data-center revenue of about $1.3 billion in 2026 and aims for well above $2 billion in 2027, followed by further growth.

Remi El-Ouazzane, head of ST’s microcontroller, digital and RF businesses, expects data-center microcontroller revenue to roughly double in 2027, while silicon photonics becomes a significantly larger contributor. STMicroelectronics plans to increase silicon-photonics capacity by more than four times year over year to support demand.

El-Ouazzane also expects the satellite business to generate revenue in 2027 at least comparable with, and potentially higher than, 2026 as existing customers expand and additional programs ramp. He said capacity, rather than demand, will likely constrain growth.

STMicroelectronics is also working with NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) on robotics, combining its sensors, microcontrollers and imaging products with NVIDIA technology to support applications from digital twins through deployed robotic systems.

Industrial And Automotive Recovery

Industrial revenue rose 40% year over year, supported by microcontrollers, analog and power-conversion products. Management highlighted design wins across factory automation, robotics, power systems and building automation.

Chéry expects automotive to contribute to company growth in 2027, supported by European electrification and design wins across electric, hybrid and internal-combustion vehicles. STMicroelectronics also expects another year of significant silicon-carbide growth as it expands beyond electric vehicles into data-center power supplies and industrial applications.

Outlook And Profitability

STMicroelectronics expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $4.15 billion, up 10.5% sequentially and 24.7% year over year (compared with the analyst consensus estimate of $4.091 billion), with gross margin around 39%. Full-year revenue is expected at roughly $14.5 billion, up 22.8% versus the $14.389 billion analyst estimate.

CFO Lorenzo Grandi said manufacturing restructuring should eventually add more than 400 basis points to gross margin, helping STMicroelectronics work toward its 44%-46% intermediate target. Better product mix, manufacturing efficiency and pricing should also support margins, although rising input costs remain a headwind.

Management also expects 2027 operating expenses to increase as STMicroelectronics accelerates investments in new growth opportunities, partly offset by roughly $100 million-$120 million of cost savings.

STM Price Action: STMicroelectronics shares were down 1.35% at $47.86 during premarket trading on Thursday, according to Benzinga Pro data.

The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s advance estimate released Thursday.

The outcome topped economists’ expectations of 3.2% and marked an acceleration from the 2.2% growth in the second quarter.

Real consumer spending grew 3.8%, the same pace as in the second quarter.

In a separate release, September’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September, matching expectations and accelerating from 3.4% in August.

On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.5%, also as expected.

Core PCE rose 3.1% year over year, in line with estimates and up from 3% previously. Month over month, core prices rose 0.3%, matching the consensus.

Personal income rose 0.2% in September, below the 0.3% forecast. Personal spending increased 0.5%, versus expectations of 0.6% and 0.9% in August.

On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at 3.75%-4.00%, pausing after the September hike.

Businesses Stocked Up as AI Spending Kept Flowing

Investment drove most of the acceleration. Companies built up inventories, led by wholesalers and manufacturers.

Equipment spending also rose, led by computers and peripheral equipment, as the AI buildout continued.

However, much of that equipment came from abroad. Imports rose faster than in the second quarter, led by capital goods.

Because GDP subtracts imports, that weighed on the headline figure. Exports fell, mainly because petroleum shipments dropped.

Fed Hike Bets Hold Steady

Shortly before the release, traders saw an 83% probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

That was little changed from 84.2% a day earlier, but up from 73.3% a week ago and 49.4% a month ago.

Interest rate swaps were little moved after the data.

Treasury Yields Hover Near 5%

The bond market took the report calmly.

The 10-year Treasury yield edged up less than 1 basis point to 5.01%, holding just above the 5% mark. The 2-year yield, which is more sensitive to Fed expectations, rose 1 basis point to 4.70%. Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was flat at 5.33%.

The U.S. dollar index was unchanged at 102.15.

Precious metals came under pressure. Spot gold fell 1.1% to around $4,025 an ounce, while silver dropped 2.8% to $52.45.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) fell 1.5% to roughly $80,040.

Big Tech Earnings Drag Nasdaq Futures

Corporate earnings, rather than macro data, drove stock moves.

Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.2%, and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.4%. Dow futures lost 0.3%. Small caps went the other way, with Russell 2000 futures up 0.3%.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 1.3% in premarket trading. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) declined 0.4%.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) was the biggest drag, sliding 11.5% to around $288. Its third-quarter report, released after Wednesday’s close, disappointed investors, even though Google Cloud grew strongly.

Software stocks sold off after earnings. Fortinet Inc. (NASDAQ:FTNT) plunged 27.6%, and ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) sank 18.3% after its outlook fell short of expectations.

Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT) dropped 11% after third-quarter revenue missed forecasts. Higher tariff costs and rising inventories also weighed on the shares. As one of the most heavily weighted stocks in the Dow, Caterpillar pulled the blue-chip index’s futures lower.

Marvell Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL) fell 12.1% on reports that it is in talks to buy Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE). Lumentum rose 5.4%.

On the upside, Carvana Co. (NYSE:CVNA) jumped 8.6% after quarterly revenue topped $8 billion for the first time. Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. (NYSE:CMG) rose 8.4% after reporting its third straight quarter of traffic growth.

A Singapore-based data center executive reportedly funneled information to Beijing while maintaining ties to Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

U.S. officials determined that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to a New York Times report on Thursday. Officials had previously suspected Huang was helping China circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips. Subsequent surveillance allegedly indicated she was also transmitting information directly to Beijing.

The surveillance reportedly documented a close relationship between Huang and Jensen Huang, raising questions about whether she obtained insight into Nvidia’s operations or U.S. policy toward China.

A Chinese businesswoman and investor, Ms. Huang, rose to a senior position at Megaspeed, a company suspected by U.S. officials of helping China circumvent export restrictions to access Nvidia computing power. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed in late 2024 after an inspection of its Malaysian data center found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising suspicions about how the chips were being handled.

President Donald Trump received a briefing about the intelligence findings about one year ago but decided against taking action. Officials reportedly believed intervention could disrupt chip sales and broader trade relations with China, according to the report.

Companies connected to Huang continued purchasing Nvidia chips this year, the report added.

An Nvidia spokesperson said in an email statement to Benzinga that, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The spokesperson added, “The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”

The spokesperson said its regional cloud customers receive "ordinary business information" rather than "sensitive Nvidia trade secrets," adding that they receive "zero information relevant to national security." The spokesperson noted that the company was confident the U.S. government would alert it if any person posed a threat to American industry. Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about "parties and entities of concern" and "always act[s] accordingly."

White House did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Nvidia Faces DOJ Scrutiny Over $12.9 Billion Hugging Face Deal Amid Concerns About Unfair AI Advantage: Report

Nvidia’s China Exposure Faces Fresh Scrutiny

The findings add new scrutiny to Nvidia’s China exposure after short-seller Culper Research alleged in May that Singapore-based Megaspeed International, identified as Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer, is secretly financed by Alibaba Group Holding (NYSE:BABA) through shell companies. The report also alleged close ties between Megaspeed’s leadership and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Culper further linked Megaspeed to a suspected server-smuggling network, citing the March 2026 DOJ indictment involving Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) and OBON Corp. The firm describes Megaspeed as the "tip of the iceberg" and flagged Aivres Systems, formerly blacklisted Inspur Systems, as a potential China-focused supply channel, raising concerns about Nvidia’s revenue exposure and the diversion of AI chips to China.

Earlier this month, Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, a contractor for Super Micro Computer, pleaded guilty to helping illegally export Nvidia AI chip-powered servers to China as part of an alleged $2.5 billion scheme.

In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) invited Jensen Huang to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about Nvidia’s U.S. export-control position and China operations. Warren argued that while Chinese purchases generate profits for American companies, they could undermine U.S. national security.

Price Action: Year-to-date, Nvidia’s stock has surged 15.49%, as per Benzinga Pro. The shares dipped 0.75% to $213.77 premarket on Thursday.

Bill Ackman’s latest investing advice offers a timely framework for ETF investors navigating AI-driven volatility: prioritize durable businesses, strong cash generation and competitive advantages over short-term earnings surprises.

In an interview on Norges Bank Investment Management CEO Nicolai Tangen’s podcast, published Wednesday, the billionaire investor argued that great businesses should remain valuable even if markets are closed for 20 years. One way to align with Ackman’s philosophy is by using ETFs to find businesses built to last as rising AI spending fuels concerns over valuations and future cash flows.

AI Spending Tests Business Quality

The stakes are growing. Major technology companies have committed enormous sums to AI infrastructure, raising questions about whether future returns will justify the spending.

For instance, Meta Platforms Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) third-quarter 2026 results illustrate the tension. Revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, but free cash flow turned negative at $2.12 billion. Capital expenditure, including finance-lease principal payments, reached $34.91 billion, while the company raised its full-year spending outlook to $135 billion to $145 billion.

For investors following Ackman’s philosophy, strong revenue growth is not enough. The bigger question is whether companies can turn heavy investment into sustainable cash generation over time.

COWZ Bets on Free Cash Flow

The Pacer US Cash Cows 100 ETF (BATS:COWZ) screens for companies with high free-cash-flow yields. The fund has approximately $19.5 billion in net assets and an expense ratio of 0.49%. Its largest holdings include Accenture PLC (NYSE:ACN), Lockheed Martin Corp. (NYSE:LMT), Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP).

COWZ’s approach aligns with Ackman’s preference for businesses that generate substantial cash. However, its portfolio is not a pure technology or AI play. Energy stocks account for approximately 20.24% of assets, while information technology represents around 20.7%.

There is a catch. High free-cash-flow yields do not necessarily indicate durable competitive advantages. Cash generation can fluctuate, and an elevated yield may reflect concerns about a company’s future growth or profitability.

MOAT Targets Competitive Advantages

The VanEck Morningstar Wide Moat ETF (BATS:MOAT) focuses on companies that Morningstar assesses as having sustainable competitive advantages.

As of Oct. 12, its holdings included Danaher Corp. (NYSE:DHR) at 2.89%, Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) at 2.82% and Estee Lauder Companies Inc. (NYSE:EL) at 2.81%.

Companies with strong brands, proprietary technology or entrenched customer relationships may enjoy pricing power and resilient demand. But even businesses with competitive moats can disappoint investors if valuations are excessive or capital spending fails to generate adequate returns.

MOAT is not an AI hedge, either. Its exposure to major technology companies leaves it vulnerable to shifts in expectations around AI investment and profitability.

Which ETF Fits Ackman’s Philosophy?

COWZ emphasizes cash generation, while MOAT prioritizes competitive advantages. Both offer frameworks for identifying potentially durable businesses, but neither guarantees attractive valuations or decades of growth.

Ackman’s own investments demonstrate that even a long-term strategy can experience sharp short-term losses when market expectations change.

For ETF investors, the takeaway is to look beyond headline returns. Comparing free-cash-flow generation, competitive advantages, valuations and capital intensity can help distinguish companies capable of compounding over time from those relying on an increasingly expensive growth story.

Google Cloud more than doubled its sales last quarter. Investors are selling Alphabet anyway.

Shares of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) sank 11% in Thursday’s premarket trading after the Google parent’s third-quarter earnings missed expectations. The stock is now on course for its worst session in more than six years.

Class A shares traded at $288.43 before the opening bell, down 11.2% from Wednesday’s $324.89 close, according to Benzinga Pro data.

If the decline holds, it would be the steepest one-day drop since March 16, 2020, when the stock lost 11.6% during the COVID-19 crash. It would also surpass the 9.5% plunge of Oct. 25, 2023, the last time an earnings report hit the shares this hard.

At current prices, the selloff would wipe out roughly $444 billion of Alphabet’s market value.

That would rank as the second-largest one-day loss for any company in stock market history.

Only Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has lost more. The chipmaker shed roughly $589 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, after the DeepSeek release rattled the AI trade.

Alphabet would also overtake Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), which gave up about $357 billion on Jan. 29, when investors balked at its AI spending.

Read Also: Nvidia Is Now Cheaper Than the Average S&P 500 Stock: Wall Street Still Sees Record Profits

Alphabet Earnings Fell Even as Revenue Jumped 25%

Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, up 24.7% from a year earlier but short of the $128.20 billion analysts had expected.

The bottom line was weaker. Net income fell 25.2% to $26.17 billion, and diluted earnings per share dropped to $2.12 from $2.87, well below the roughly $3 consensus.

However, Search is where investors are focused.

Search and other advertising revenue grew 12%, slowing from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second. Paid clicks rose 8%, cost per click increased 4% and network revenue was nearly flat.

In addition, management flagged larger foreign-exchange headwinds in the fourth quarter, particularly for Search and YouTube ads, as well as tougher comparisons against a strong year-earlier period.

Google Cloud Growth Is Not Enough for Alphabet Stock

The cloud business told a different story. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, helped by infrastructure demand and sales of Tensor Processing Units, Google’s custom AI chips, which it now sells as full systems.

Executives said nearly 100 clients currently use TPUs. They also expect to recognize just over 55% of the cloud backlog as revenue over the next 24 months.

Meanwhile, the spending bill keeps climbing. Alphabet’s capital expenditures reached $132 billion in the first nine months of 2026, and the company left its full-year capex forecast unchanged.

That tension was exactly what investors were weighing overnight.

“Google just released maybe the most disappointing Earnings in its history. I don’t say that lightly,” Michael Spencer wrote in his AI Supremacy newsletter on Thursday.

Spencer argued that Alphabet is finally diversifying beyond advertising through TPUs and Google Cloud. However, he warned that the shift comes at a cost.

“The transition is so bumpy, you’d be hard pressed not to question the plan,” he wrote.

The bigger worry, in his view, is what AI is doing to Search itself. Google query volumes remain high, but fewer of those searches send users to outside websites.

“How do you monetize zero click journeys well? It’s the beginning of the end of an era,” Spencer wrote.

Read Also: Anthropic Publicly Files for IPO: What Will ANT Stock Be Worth on Day One?

Nasdaq Futures Feel the Hit

Alphabet’s slide weighed on the broader tech complex.

Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.1%, while S&P 500 futures slipped 0.3%.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) dropped 1.1% premarket. The State Street Communication Services Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLC), where Alphabet is a top holding, lost 1.7%.

The size of the record now depends on the close. A finish below about $287.11 would make Thursday’s loss deeper than the March 2020 drop.

Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya and Citadel LLC Founder and CEO Ken Griffin supported a financial framework that equates the artificial intelligence (AI) GPU market to the commercial airline industry. The model compares GPU manufacturers to aircraft builders and AI compute capacity to airline inventory.

The AI Aviation Model

The analogy gained public traction following a publication by Alex Song, co-founder of Made Card and former asset-backed securities trader, who wrote, “A GPU neocloud has basically the same operating model as an airline.” Song asserted that hardware manufacturers control the market surplus, stating that “Nvidia [Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA)] is Boeing [Boeing Co. (NYSE: BA)] and Airbus rolled into one.”

According to Song’s framework, AI cloud providers lock in high fixed infrastructure costs while selling compute on demand, leaving profitability entirely dependent on hardware utilization.

Read Also: Ken Griffin Says We’re ‘Almost Certainly’ in an AI Bubble, Recalls How Past Bubbles Created Market Leaders for Decades: ‘I Just Wish I’d Kept My Amazon Stock’

Endorsements from Executives

On Wednesday, Palihapitiya shared Song’s post on the social media platform X, stating it is a “Super interesting comparison of GPU finance and the AI buildout to airlines.”

Palihapitiya noted that Griffin and Snowflake Inc. (NYSE:SNOW) CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy had made the identical comparison, adding, “Both are very, very smart so worth learning more.”

Griffin previously outlined the economic risks of this structure. According to reports of his Oct. 21 conference appearance, Griffin stated, “GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run,” warning that “the moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall.”

Perishability and Financing Risks

Ramaswamy also detailed the similarities in an Oct. 28 social media thread. Comparing AI compute to flight inventory, Ramaswamy stated that “airlines lease planes for years and sell seats one flight at a time.” He noted the perishability of both assets, writing, “an empty seat at takeoff is gone forever. so is yesterday’s unused GPU-hour.”

Song’s analysis further compares data centers to airframes and GPUs to aircraft engines. According to Song, a debt-financed GPU cluster requires “roughly 65% to 75% utilization” to cover fixed costs. Ramaswamy concluded his industry analysis by warning that due to this financial setup, “a capacity bust is more likely than a bank run.”

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) is heading back to the U.S. investment-grade bond market for the first time since 2017. 

The company is looking to raise at least $25 billion through as many as 10 tranches, with maturities stretching from two to 40 years, Bloomberg first reported Thursday.  

  • MSFT stock is moving after earnings. Get all the details first. 

The final size remains open and could move with demand. Early price talk on the longest-dated piece, a note due in 2066, sits as much as 1.35 percentage points above Treasuries, according to Reuters. 

Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase and UBS Group are managing the sale, with proceeds slated for general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures.

Nine years is a long gap between debt raises. Microsoft’s last high-grade deal raised $17 billion in 2017. Moody’s Ratings and S&P Global Ratings both rate the company AAA, a grade held by only one other publicly traded U.S. company, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ).

Spending Outpaces the Cash Pile

The return to debt markets follows a quarter of heavy investment. Microsoft booked $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases in the September quarter, roughly 30% above a year earlier, while Azure revenue climbed 48% to $33.2 billion. 

CFO Amy Hood told analysts the company is aiming for more than $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter spending and $170 billion across calendar 2027, citing capacity constraints. 

Read Also: Lumentum Stock Soars 17% on Marvell Takeover Talk

Big Tech’s Borrowing Binge

Microsoft is arriving late to an already crowded debt party. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) went to market on Aug. 6 seeking as much as $25 billion in up to 10 parts, with maturities of two to 40 years, a structure nearly identical to Microsoft’s. 

Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) combined sold about $194 billion of bonds in 2026 through July 7, a 79% jump from roughly $108 billion in 2025, according to a Reuters analysis. 

Oracle has leaned on outside capital harder than most. The company said in February it would raise up to $50 billion in 2026 through stock and debt sales to expand its cloud infrastructure business. 

Analysts at Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan have projected the tech sector could issue as much as $1.5 trillion in new debt over the next few years to fund AI and data center projects, Axios reported. 

CoreWeave Borrows on Different Terms

Further down the credit spectrum sits CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV). The AI cloud provider launched a $3 billion convertible debt offering in September, with initial buyers able to purchase up to $500 million more. 

CoreWeave has described its financing moves as part of an effort to reach an investment-grade credit profile. Microsoft already sits at the very top of the scale. The distance between the two borrowers shows how sharply the cost of funding the AI boom varies depending on who is asking. 

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Bond Buyers Grow Selective

Credit investors have grown choosy. Worries about AI-related debt have eased lately after a volatile stretch, CNBC reported Tuesday. 

Meta’s plan for a $95 billion stock offering helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads, which had risen after the company posted negative free cash flow in the third quarter. 

Richard Cheng, who heads Nuveen’s investment-grade corporate sector team, said investors had expected a large Meta bond deal, and the absence of one helped tighten AI-related spreads. Still, CDS spreads remain wider than a year ago, reflecting a surge in issuance and negative free cash flow across parts of the AI space.

Microsoft arrives with an edge few peers can match — its AAA rating should draw a deep order book. Even so, demand for the 40-year note will offer a clear read on how much extra yield bond buyers now want to finance the AI buildout. Even from a AAA borrower.

Billionaire investor Mark Cuban says personalized social media feeds increasingly shape how Americans understand politics, technology, and public debate.

Cuban took to X on Wednesday and stated that conversations with Texas-based Gen Z professionals and college graduates revealed that they had “no idea” about Senate candidates for the state, Democrat James Talarico or Republican Ken Paxton.

The Shark Tank star argued that social media algorithms influence thinking more than other forces because every user receives a distinct feed. He compared those feeds to fingerprints, saying no two are alike.

Cuban Says AI Algorithms Fuel Divisiveness

In a a16z podcast episode on Wednesday, Cuban said, "What controls how pretty much everybody in this country thinks right now? Social media algorithms." He said users receive more of what they already seek.

Cuban said effective AI marketing requires understanding and “reverse-engineer” these algorithms rather than relying on traditional advertising. The speaker also highlighted the irony that AI-powered algorithms contribute to social “divisiveness,” and is impacting every area of life such as sports, politics and more.

"It’s useless when you’re trying to change hearts and minds about AI specifically. Even though the irony of it all is that it’s the AI behind the algorithms that’s ruining everything.”

Meta Blocks Rival Ads As AI Competition Grows

Cuban’s remarks come as major technology companies compete for advertising budgets while algorithmic personalization shapes audience attention. Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) recently barred ByteDance from advertising on Facebook and Instagram across seven countries, including the U.S. Meta said it would not run ads for competitors seeking to draw users away from its platforms, calling the decision a normal business practice. The company said it would continue competing through product quality and user experience.

“Panther Lake / 18A” sits at 98%. Panther Lake is Intel’s first PC platform built on 18A, its advanced 2-nanometer-class manufacturing process designed to challenge TSMC. Intel hopes to eventually manufacture chips for other companies, turning its expensive factories into a profitable business.

“Security” trades at 93%, while “Fortinet” sits at just 25%. Intel agreed in July to manufacture a chip for cybersecurity company Fortinet (NASDAQ:FTNT), its first publicly named outside foundry customer under Tan.

“Desktop” stands at 70%, even as global desktop shipments fell 23.5% in the third quarter, according to Omdia.

“Apple” is at 12%. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) has been floated as a potential foundry customer, but neither company has confirmed a deal.

The odds point to a gap between Intel’s manufacturing ambitions and the outside customers needed to pay for them.

Options traders are pricing a roughly 9% post-earnings move, equivalent to about $45 billion in market value.

Investors will be listening for evidence that a major customer is ready to commit.

Steve Eisman believes the AI boom has a weak link: OpenAI and Anthropic are spending billions on computing power, but cheaper rival models could force them to cut prices, threatening their ability to keep spending.

“The whole chain depends upon the health of Anthropic and OpenAI at least at this point,” the Big Short investor told CNBC Thursday morning, warning that chipmakers and cloud providers are exposed to their financial fortunes.

Asked Wednesday whether he’d buy Anthropic’s IPO, Eisman’s answer was simply: “No.”

But Morningstar argues that the enormous scale of the two frontier labs could protect them. By buying computing power in bulk, the biggest AI labs can secure prices smaller competitors cannot match, potentially giving them a $57 billion annual cost advantage.

Morningstar’s $57 Billion Counterargument

In October Morningstar analysts estimated that multiyear agreements could secure Nvidia B200 computing capacity for $2.25 per GPU-hour, versus a $16.11 hyperscaler list price.

For a gigawatt of computing power, that’s an annual bill of roughly $9 billion instead of $66 billion, an illustrative $57 billion saving.

“The labs are the only buyers able to commit at that duration and scale,” Morningstar wrote.

The analysts see another advantage in Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex: more customers generate feedback that can improve the products and encourage users to stay.

But cheaper computing doesn’t guarantee customers will keep paying premium prices.

Customers Are Already Shopping Around

October data from Vercel shows customers are increasingly spreading their AI spending across competing models.

Anthropic captured 44% of spending through Vercel’s AI Gateway in September, down from 64% just a month earlier.

But the overall market is booming. Spending on the most advanced AI models has grown tenfold since December, even as cheaper alternatives gain ground.

That means AI companies can grow rapidly while losing market share, raising questions about how much they will eventually be able to charge.

Anthropic’s Oct. 26 IPO filing showed $11.56 billion in second-quarter revenue and $974 million in operating profit, but warned that cheaper rivals could put pressure on prices.

Polymarket Traders Price a $2 Trillion Debut

On Polymarket, traders see roughly a 56% chance that Anthropic will end its first day of trading valued between $1.75 trillion and $2.25 trillion. The market has attracted more than $2 million in trading volume.

The valuations suggest traders expect a huge debut, even as Eisman questions whether Anthropic can defend its margins.

Why Microsoft and Amazon Are Exposed

Eisman has previously estimated, citing Wall Street research, that OpenAI and Anthropic account for roughly 70% of hyperscalers’ AI revenue.

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) has invested $18 billion in Anthropic and $50 billion in OpenAI, according to its second-quarter filing. Anthropic, in turn, has committed more than $100 billion to Amazon’s cloud infrastructure over the next decade.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) disclosed an approximately 25% stake in OpenAI and reported $24.1 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue from commercial arrangements with the company, including revenue-sharing payments.

For both technology giants, Eisman’s warning goes beyond the value of their investments. Their cloud businesses also depend on AI labs continuing to spend heavily.

Investors are shifting toward dividend and quality-focused ETFs as selling in individual US stocks intensifies, according to Bank of America’s latest equity client flow report.

Bank of America clients pulled a net $3.526 billion from individual stocks in the week covered by its Tuesday report, after record outflows of about $15 billion the previous week. Stock ETFs, however, attracted $2.345 billion in net inflows for a second consecutive week, even as the S&P 500 fell 0.5%.

The divergence suggests investors are reducing company-specific risk without abandoning equity exposure altogether.

Dividend and Quality ETF Flows Strengthen

Bank of America said the four-week average of dividend ETF inflows reached a near-year high, while quality and multi-factor ETF inflows climbed to their highest level since tracking began in August 2025. Momentum ETFs, meanwhile, experienced outflows.

The trend points to growing interest in strategies emphasizing income, profitability and other fundamental characteristics over stocks driven by recent price momentum.

Meta Selloff Triggers Record Sector Outflows

Communication services stocks recorded $4.786 billion in net outflows, the largest weekly withdrawal since the sector classification was introduced in September 2018. The selling followed Meta Platforms Inc’s (NASDAQ:META) post-earnings slump.

Technology stocks also saw $931 million in net outflows, while industrials recorded $1.232 billion in withdrawals, extending their selling streak to 13 consecutive weeks.

Yet technology ETFs attracted $317 million, suggesting some investors continued to seek sector exposure through diversified funds rather than individual companies.

3 ETFs That Align With The Rotation

  • Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSE:SCHD) focuses on dividend-paying US companies selected using fundamental measures, including dividend sustainability. Its 0.06% expense ratio makes it a relevant example of the income-oriented strategy gaining traction.
  • Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSE:VIG) tracks companies with a record of increasing dividends over time. With a 0.04% expense ratio, it offers exposure to dividend growth rather than simply targeting the highest current yields.
  • JPMorgan U.S. Quality Factor ETF (NYSE:JQUA) selects US stocks based on characteristics including profitability, solvency and earnings quality. Its 0.12% expense ratio makes it a direct fit for the quality-factor theme highlighted in Bank of America’s report.

These funds illustrate the strategies attracting interest; Bank of America did not identify them as specific client purchases.

What The Rotation Means For Investors

Bank of America clients recorded combined net outflows of $1.181 billion from stocks and ETFs last week. Year to date, individual stocks have suffered $9.81 billion in net outflows, while ETFs have attracted $6.31 billion.

The shift toward dividend and quality ETFs suggests investors are becoming more selective about equity exposure as earnings risks and AI-related uncertainty persist.

Whether the trend continues will depend on whether these funds sustain their inflows while momentum strategies remain under pressure.

For investors, the key question is not simply which ETFs attract money, but whether the underlying companies can deliver durable earnings and cash flows if market volatility intensifies.

The last time value stocks beat the S&P 500 this decisively in a single month, the dot-com bubble was coming apart.

The iShares Russell 1000 Value ETF (NYSE:IWD) is up 5% in October and touched a record high of $260.64 on Thursday.

Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) has gained just 0.8% over the same stretch.

That 4.2-percentage-point gap is the widest monthly outperformance for value since February 2001, in data going back to IWD’s launch in 2000.

Against growth, the split is even wider.

The iShares Russell 1000 Growth ETF (NYSE:IWF) is down 3.3% this month. Year to date, IWD is up 23.8%, while IWF has gained only 2.4%.

Wall Street Is Rotating, Not Retreating

Thursday’s session showed the shift in real time.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) fell 12% after a disappointing third-quarter report. ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) sank 25% on slower contract growth guidance.

On the same day, however, the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLV) touched an all-time high.

Read Also: ServiceNow Stock Plunges on Worst Day in Company’s History: AI Wins Can’t Hide a Bookings Slowdown

Investors are “increasingly distinguishing between companies successfully monetizing AI and those still incurring significant capital expenditures without a clear revenue or cash flow payoff,” Chris Osmond, chief investment officer at Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, said in emailed comments.

“The resulting environment favors selectivity: current cash flow over distant promises, balance-sheet strength over leverage, and companies that can demonstrate AI monetization rather than simply announce higher AI investment,” Osmond added.

February 2001: When The New Economy Ran Out Of Road

In early 2001, the Federal Reserve had already cut rates twice, and many investors treated the tech selloff as a buying opportunity. February proved them wrong.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) lost 26.2% that month, IWF dropped 17.8% and SPY fell 9.5%. IWD, by contrast, slipped just 2.7%.

Leadership changed hands. Stocks priced for perfection were repriced, while companies with ordinary earnings at ordinary valuations held their ground.

Why 2026 Is Not A Carbon Copy

In February 2001, value won because everything else fell faster. This October, value is rising in absolute terms, and the S&P 500 is still positive for the month.

In other words, money is moving within the market, not leaving it.

The rate backdrop also runs the other way. The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00% on Wednesday after raising them in September, and two policymakers dissented in favor of another hike.

As a result, the pressure falls hardest on companies whose value rests on profits far in the future.

“There are mounting signs of markets becoming increasingly unwilling to fund the AI infrastructure build-out,” Sebastian Raedler, investment strategist at Bank of America, said in an Oct. 23 Bank of America Global Research report.

Dennis DeBusschere of 22V Research made a similar point in an Oct. 27 note: “Cash return is scarcer now because of the capital committed to the AI buildout.”

Read Also: Alphabet Stock Set for Worst Day Since March 2020: Search Slowdown Overshadows Cloud Boom

The Question February 2001 Leaves Open

Not everyone sees a broader top forming.

“We don’t believe stocks are about to go into a bear market, despite all of the angst we’ve seen and heard this month about Cap Ex spending,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, said in emailed comments.

Still, in 2001 value stocks’ best month against the market came early in a multiyear leadership change, not at its end.

Whether October 2026 opens a similar cycle depends on one thing Wall Street can’t price yet: how fast AI spending turns into AI revenue.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is stalling for the same reason it did before the SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) IPO, analyst Benjamin Cowen says, pointing to capital rotating out of crypto ahead of Anthropic’s listing.

Why Bitcoin Looks Like It’s Repeating the SpaceX Playbook

Cowen said on the NFA Live podcast that Bitcoin’s current price action looks "almost the exact same" as its drawdown in the 30 days before SpaceX’s IPO, based on a normalized return chart comparing both periods. 

He expects Anthropic’s IPO to land the week of November 16 to 20, with investors possibly holding capital back now to deploy into that listing. 

He pointed to the S&P 500’s (NYSE:SPY) roughly 5% drop ahead of the SpaceX IPO as a similar precedent.

Cowen said he expects long-term Treasury yields to spike into the midterms before dropping shortly afterward, drawing a direct parallel to 2018, when the Fed paused rate hikes around that year’s midterms before raising rates again in December despite a falling stock market. 

He noted the Fed’s December 2018 projections pointed to two rate hikes in 2019 that never materialized, and said the market currently prices in two hikes for 2027 that could similarly get priced out if growth concerns take over from inflation concerns.

Why AI-Driven Bank Hacks Are an Underpriced Risk

Panelist Rob pointed to a wave of AI-assisted bank hacks hitting seven countries at once:

  • Latin America: a gang used Claude, Grok and Kimi to steal banking credentials
  • Japan: hackers breached GMO’s currency trading service and demanded $50 million in crypto

He called the scale of these attacks unprecedented compared to anything seen before.

Cowen flagged a more technical risk: recent OpenAI research disproving the exponential time hypothesis, a mathematical assumption underlying much of modern cryptography. 

He said if similar research eventually challenges the broader P versus NP problem, it could theoretically threaten the computational difficulty that blockchain security relies on, though he stressed that outcome remains purely speculative for now.

Why the Panel Expects Midterm Volatility to Fade by 2027

Cowen expects the S&P 500 to stay rangebound until the midterms, followed by a potential final drop before markets rebound heading into 2027. 

Rob cited Polymarket data showing a 68% implied probability that Democrats retake the Senate, noting prediction markets have recently missed high-confidence outcomes in Brazil, Serbia and Israel. 

Both analysts said continued uncertainty around the Iran conflict and upcoming AI-sector IPOs will likely keep volatility elevated through the rest of the fourth quarter.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wants Americans to own half of major AI developers, including Anthropic, which filed for an IPO Monday, and OpenAI. A new CNN poll shows him leading Michigan’s Senate race by seven points.

The survey released Thursday puts El-Sayed ahead of Republican Mike Rogers, 49% to 42%, among 768 likely voters, with a 4.7-point margin of error.

On Polymarket, traders put El-Sayed’s election chances near 72%, with about $3 million traded. His polling lead exceeds the 3.2-point average tracked by RealClearPolling.

Americans Would Own Half of AI Giants

El-Sayed backs Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-VT) proposal to impose a one-time 50% stock tax on AI companies with more than $200 million in annual AI sales, paid in newly issued shares.

The shares would enter a public sovereign wealth fund that Sanders estimates could be worth $7 trillion. He says an annual payout equal to 5% of the fund’s value could provide every American with more than $1,000.

“I want to actually take it a step further,” El-Sayed said in June when asked about Sanders’ public-ownership proposal.

His platform would give publicly appointed or elected directors a majority of board seats at frontier AI companies.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) owns about 24% of OpenAI. Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) owns an estimated 9% of Anthropic, while Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) holds at least 6.6%, according to Bloomberg.

Under Sanders’ proposal, Microsoft’s stake in OpenAI would fall to about 12%. Google and Amazon would see their percentage ownership in Anthropic halved too.

El-Sayed’s expanded October plan also seeks to pause frontier AI development and new data centers until safety standards are established. Rogers separately supports a one-year moratorium on new Michigan data centers.

University of Michigan professor Elizabeth Anderson told PolitiFact the mandatory equity transfer “sounds like outright expropriation,” questioning its constitutionality. Sanders’ legislation has not passed Congress.

Anthropic Pledges 5%, El-Sayed Wants 50%

Anthropic announced October 18 that it would dedicate an initial 5% of its shares to a wholly owned public-benefit fund, subject to shareholder approval.

The fund could finance charitable grants or direct payments to specific populations. Unlike El-Sayed’s proposal, Anthropic would retain control over the fund.

Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Its formal investor roadshow could begin as early as November 10, one week after Michigan voters choose their next senator.

Wants Answers From Huang

U.S. officials determined that Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence asset, and surveillance reportedly documented a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, the New York Times reported Thursday.

President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago but decided against acting, the report said.

“Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers,” the Senator said in a post on X Thursday.

An Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga that Megaspeed is “no different than many other regional cloud customers” and that Huang talks with “thousands of customer executives every year.”

Chris McGuire of the Council on Foreign Relations said that the report shows chip diversion to China through Southeast Asia is as bad as many have asserted, and that Commerce Department and Nvidia are doing little to stop it.

He called it “undoubtedly the largest illegal transfer of controlled technology in world history.”

In a post on X, Cramer said he was “disappointed in Intel,” which he named his favorite stock earlier this year, adding that he was “actually furious about it.”

Moor Insights & Strategy CEO Patrick Moorhead called it a “good” quarter with a “very challenging guide.”

Author and investor Jeff Macke questioned “the point of the government taking over companies if we are going to let them miss estimates.”

Memory Costs Hit PC Demand

Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster said PC demand is the main issue, with the company pointing to high memory costs as the reason demand is slowing.

He added that Intel’s weak guide should not be applied to Nvidia Corp. which has been beating estimates despite high memory costs.

Former BlackRock Inc. portfolio manager Edward Dowd called the hit to PC demand from higher memory prices as “demand destruction.”

Not a Demand Issue, Some Analysts Say

Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman said the weak guide “isn’t a demand issue” and is more about “expanding capacity and perhaps mix shift.”

Futurum’s market strategist Shay Boloor noted that Intel’s CEO Lip-Bu Tan cited “extraordinary demand” for its Xeon family but named production yields, substrate shortages and an Israel factory shutdown as headwinds limiting shipments.

The timing is bad, Boloor said, with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia pushing deeper into server CPUs, where losing a customer today could cost years of future business.

Beats on Q3, Guides Below Estimates

Intel reported third quarter earnings of 52 cents per share, which beat the consensus estimate of 40 cents by 30%, per Benzinga Pro data. Revenue came in at $16.51 billion, which beat the analyst estimate of $16.47 billion.

The company expects fourth-quarter adjusted EPS of 25 cents, versus the 43-cent analyst estimate, and revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, versus the $17.05 billion estimate.

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) and SanDisk Corp. (NASDAQ:SNDK) remain well below their 2026 highs even as memory-industry profits climb, prompting Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya to question whether memory is becoming a more durable "franchise" or heading for another boom-and-bust commodity cycle.

Palihapitiya wrote that "memory chip profits are exploding," while questioning why the stocks remain below their highs.

Profits Surge, Stocks Lag

Palihapitiya said Micron’s fiscal 2026 revenue reached $133.2 billion, up 256% from $37.4 billion in fiscal 2025, a faster one-year increase than Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) posted in any recent year.

A Social Capital chart shared with the post shows Micron’s fiscal 2026 GAAP gross margin at 80.7%, compared with negative 9% in fiscal 2023. Palihapitiya said memory makers have become major beneficiaries of the superintelligence, or SI, boom.

The accompanying stock-performance chart shows Micron 23% below its 2026 high as of the Oct. 29 close and SanDisk 43% below its high. Social Capital showed SK Hynix 48% below its high, Samsung 36% lower, and Kioxia 60% lower.

Read Also: 'Nvidia is Boeing': Chamath Palihapitiya and Ken Griffin Back Viral Analogy Comparing AI GPUs to Airlines

Cycle Or Franchise?

Palihapitiya said memory has historically been a commodity business in which profits were difficult to protect, while arguing that successive industry eras may be changing the economics.

He also pointed to a familiar risk: producers are using record cash generation to expand capacity, with new factories scheduled from 2027 through 2029. Palihapitiya said China’s CXMT is also expanding, citing Counterpoint data showing its global DRAM revenue share rising from 4% to 10% in a year.

That leaves what Palihapitiya framed as the central question: is memory becoming a "franchise," or is the industry positioned for another boom-and-bust cycle?

What Could End The Boom

Palihapitiya cautioned that another downturn would not require SI demand to stop growing. He said the prior two memory downturns began when customers worked through accumulated inventory, causing orders to pause while suppliers faced lower prices and shipments.

With customers now putting up billions of dollars in deposits to secure supply, Palihapitiya said whether memory becomes a franchise or returns to a commodity cycle is the question that determines the industry’s trajectory.

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) shares plunged about 25.60% in Friday’s pre-market trading, putting the stock on course for its worst single-day decline in more than two years, even as CEO Lip-Bu Tan predicted artificial intelligence (AI) agents could drive the server CPU market beyond $200 billion.

Intel’s Earnings Beat Overshadowed By Weak Outlook

Intel reported third-quarter revenue of $16.51 billion, up 21%, and adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, exceeding analysts’ expectations of 40 cents. If this decline holds during Friday’s regular trading session, the stock would be on track for its worst single-day performance in more than two years.

However, Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below Wall Street’s $17.07 billion estimate. Its 25-cent adjusted earnings outlook also disappointed investors. Reuters reported that an explosion at Intel’s Israeli factory could reduce revenue by approximately $600 million over two quarters. Rising memory costs and weakening PC demand added pressure.

Lip-Bu Tan Predicts Fivefold CPU Market Expansion

"The resurgence in demand for CPU is a meaningful tailwind for us along our transformation journey," Tan told analysts during Thursday’s earnings call.

Read Also: Shopify CEO Doesn't Trust the AI Cloud With His Data — So He Built a Server in His Wine Cellar

"While GPUs are great at thinking tasks, deterministic CPUs are more efficient at doing tasks," he added, emphasizing energy efficiency as AI agents increasingly execute computational workloads. "By our estimates, server CPU TAM, largely driven by agentic workloads, could increase as much as five times from where it is today, from $40 billion to more than $200 billion over five years. This makes the opportunity for Intel enormous."

Intel also expanded its collaboration with Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) to support enterprise and agentic AI workloads using Xeon processors.

Analysts Weigh Strong Demand Against Supply Constraints

Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman argued Intel’s weak guidance "isn’t a demand issue," pointing instead to capacity expansion and product mix.

However, Futurum strategist Shay Boloor warned that production constraints could allow Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) to capture server CPU customers.

Meanwhile, Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg told Reuters on Thursday, following Intel’s third-quarter earnings, "I think we entered earnings season with the market in a pessimistic mood. No result is good enough, and bad results receive extra punishment."

Intel’s data-center business nevertheless delivered its strongest revenue growth in 15 years, according to management. The company must now expand manufacturing capacity to capitalize on Tan’s projected AI opportunity.
